performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
intro: A bird announces spring; the drinker would prefer another cup. Carl Martin Öhmann sings this unruly little drama with the Concertgebouw Orchestra and Carl Schuricht in their live 1939 Das Lied von der Erde.

sections.label: A · The drinker’s crooked dance
sections.mNote: Trilling winds and horns begin without the strings

sections.label: B · A bird outside the door
sections.mNote: Solo violin, flute and harp interrupt the drinking

sections.label: A′ · The cup is filled again
sections.mNote: Harp arpeggios and plucked cellos restore the first tempo

cues.title: A drinker’s first question
cues.text: Oboes and clarinets trill above the horns; the strings wait. Öhmann enters with a question: “Wenn nur ein Traum das Leben ist” — if life is only a dream. Why bother with toil and trouble? The horn figures keep tripping over their grace notes.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), p. 81: opening wind and brass scoring, grace notes and tenor entry in bar 5. Hans Bethge’s text; our translation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bird wakes him
cues.text: The drinker wakes to birdsong. A solo violin curls above the softened orchestra; the flute answers, and the harp joins. “Ein Vogel singt im Baum” — a bird sings in the tree. Mahler holds back the pace around this small discovery.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 86: solo violin, flute, harp, Noch ruhiger and Zurückhaltend. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Is spring here already?
cues.text: The tenor asks whether spring has come. His repeated “mir ist” hesitates before “als wie im Traum” — as though in a dream. The solo violin and harp give the question space, with only a few low winds and strings beneath.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 87: Rit., Langsam, the tenor’s question, solo violin, harp and reduced accompaniment. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A moment with the bird
cues.text: For a moment the drinker stays with the birdsong. D♭ major opens beneath his quiet line, and Mahler writes “Zögernd” and “Ganz langsam” — hesitant, very slow. Muted strings, bassoons and horns sustain the stillness around him.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 89–90: five-flat signature, Zögernd, Ganz langsam and sustained muted strings, horns and bassoons.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another cup wins
cues.text: “Ich fülle mir den Becher neu” — I fill my cup again. The first tempo snaps back. Harp arpeggios and plucked cellos set the drinker on his feet, and the violins have taken off their mutes. He sings on until the moon appears.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 91–92: Tempo I subito, Dämpfer ab, harp and pizzicato cellos. Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Spring can wait
cues.text: “Laßt mich betrunken sein!” — let me be drunk! Öhmann’s final answer dismisses the bird and its good news. An A-major Allegro sends woodwind runs tumbling over string chords; triangle and trumpet join the last flourish.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 95–96, rehearsal 14: final words, Allegro and A-major orchestral ending. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A solo violin wakes the drinker
transitions.to: B · A bird outside the door
transitions.how: The drinker’s sleep gives way to a solo violin and quiet wind figures in A major. Noch ruhiger, then Zurückhaltend, slows his waking question. The harp enters with soft chords as the tenor locates the bird in its tree.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 85–86: waking stanza, solo violin, harp and the two tempo markings.

transitions.title: Plucked cellos refill the cup
transitions.from: B · A bird outside the door
transitions.to: A′ · The cup is filled again
transitions.how: The D♭-major pause begins to flow again at Etwas fließender. The strings remove their mutes. The tenor’s “Ich” leads straight into Tempo I subito, where harp arpeggios and plucked cellos accompany his freshly filled cup.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 90–91, rehearsal figures 9–10: D♭ major, Etwas fließender, Dämpfer ab and Tempo I subito.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, V. Der Trunkene im Frühling, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 81–96: wind-and-brass opening, solo violin and flute in the bird scene, harp and plucked cellos at the refilled cup.

timeline.note: Oboes and clarinets trill over horn and trumpet figures; the strings are silent.
The tenor enters over the winds and brass.
Strings join in pizzicato and arco as the tenor asks why toil and trouble.
Triangle and trumpet join the full band for “Ich trinke, bis ich nicht mehr kann”.
Solo violin and flute answer the tenor’s waking question; the harp enters as he names the bird.
Langsam: harp, solo violin and a few solo strings, with low winds beneath the tenor’s question.
The bird answers “Ja!”: woodwind trills, a muted trumpet, triangle and the solo violin’s harmonics.
Zögernd, ganz langsam: muted strings, horns and bassoons under the tenor’s “Aus tiefstem Schauen”.
Tempo I subito: harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos as the cup is refilled.
Harp glissandi and string harmonics surround the moonlit end of the tenor’s phrase.
Quieter again as he falls asleep: solo violin returns with winds and strings.
Woodwind runs tumble over string chords; triangle and trumpet join the final flourish.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
